eSVD2: master (3d5f7bf) versus devel (1.2.0) on simulated cohorts

Drafted by Claude for Kevin Z. Lin

2026-09-29

library(ggplot2)
out_dir <- "output"
version_vec <- c("master", "devel", "devel_nocap", "devel_swap")

gene_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(version_vec, function(v){
  utils::read.csv(file.path(out_dir, v, "genes.csv"))
}))
truth_df <- utils::read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "truth.csv"))
gene_df <- merge(gene_df, truth_df, by = c("regime", "rep", "gene"))
gene_df$p <- 10^(-gene_df$log10p)
gene_df$status <- factor(ifelse(gene_df$is_de, "DE", "null"),
                         levels = c("null", "DE"))

# The rate shares units with the fitted library size, which contains the
# gene's intercept; the generator's library averages 1. Multiplying the true
# rate by the gene's median fitted library size (stored by 1.2.0, and the same
# fit under every devel arm) puts both on the fit's scale.
library_df <- gene_df[gene_df$version == "devel",
                      c("regime", "rep", "gene", "nuisance_library_median")]
colnames(library_df)[4] <- "s_median"
gene_df <- merge(gene_df[, colnames(gene_df) != "nuisance_library_median"],
                 library_df, by = c("regime", "rep", "gene"))
gene_df$nuisance_true_fit <- gene_df$nuisance_true * gene_df$s_median

run_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(version_vec, function(v){
  utils::read.csv(file.path(out_dir, v, "runs.csv"))
}))
corner_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("master", "devel"), function(v){
  utils::read.csv(file.path(out_dir, v, "corner_cases.csv"))
}))
wall_time_df <- utils::read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "wall_time.csv"),
                                header = FALSE)

# One row per gene per data set, with the versions side by side.
.wide <- function(column){
  res <- gene_df[gene_df$version == "master",
                 c("regime", "rep", "gene", "status", column)]
  colnames(res)[5] <- "master"
  for(v in setdiff(version_vec, "master")){
    tmp_df <- gene_df[gene_df$version == v, c("regime", "rep", "gene", column)]
    colnames(tmp_df)[4] <- v
    res <- merge(res, tmp_df, by = c("regime", "rep", "gene"))
  }
  res
}

regime_levels <- c("baseline", "null", "strong_de", "near_poisson",
                   "minimal_design", "generate_null")
version_col_vec <- c(master = "#2a78d6", devel = "#eb6834",
                     devel_nocap = "#9e9d97", devel_swap = "#1baf7a")
status_col_vec <- c(null = "#9e9d97", DE = "#4a3aa7")
nuisance_status_col_vec <- c(estimated = "#2a78d6", capped = "#eb6834",
                             boundary = "#4a3aa7")

theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 11))
theme_update(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
             strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f1f0ec", colour = NA))
num_null_genes <- sum(!gene_df$is_de & gene_df$version == "master" &
                        gene_df$regime == "null") / 10
.fp_per_rep <- function(v, r){
  idx <- gene_df$version == v & gene_df$regime == r
  sum(gene_df$fdr[idx] < 0.05 & !gene_df$is_de[idx]) / 10
}
.tp_per_rep <- function(v, r){
  idx <- gene_df$version == v & gene_df$regime == r
  sum(gene_df$fdr[idx] < 0.05 & gene_df$is_de[idx]) / 10
}
.type1 <- function(v, r){
  idx <- gene_df$version == v & gene_df$regime == r & !gene_df$is_de
  mean(gene_df$p[idx] < 0.05)
}
.within_twofold <- function(v){
  idx <- gene_df$version == v & gene_df$regime %in%
    c("baseline", "null", "strong_de", "minimal_design")
  mean(abs(log2(gene_df$nuisance[idx] / gene_df$nuisance_true_fit[idx])) <= 1)
}
logfc_wide_df <- .wide("logFC")
min_logfc_cor <- min(sapply(split(logfc_wide_df, logfc_wide_df$regime),
                            function(x){stats::cor(x$master, x$devel)}))
teststat_wide_df <- .wide("teststat")
min_teststat_cor <- min(sapply(split(teststat_wide_df, teststat_wide_df$regime),
                               function(x){stats::cor(x$master, x$devel)}))
swap_max <- max(abs(teststat_wide_df$master - teststat_wide_df$devel_swap))

devel_df <- gene_df[gene_df$version == "devel", ]
ordinary_vec <- c("baseline", "null", "strong_de", "minimal_design",
                  "generate_null")
frac_capped_vec <- sapply(ordinary_vec, function(r){
  mean(devel_df$nuisance_status[devel_df$regime == r] %in%
         c("capped", "boundary"))
})

1 Overview

This report compares two versions of eSVD2 on the same simulated data:

  • master: git commit 3d5f7bf, DESCRIPTION version 1.0.1.07. This is what devtools::install_github("linnykos/eSVD2") installs today.
  • devel: the devel branch at commit 1a0a536, version 1.2.0, the candidate for CRAN. It caps each gene’s nuisance rate at 10 times the median of its library size (cap_multiplier = 10, the default).

A third arm, devel_nocap, is 1.2.0 run with cap_multiplier = Inf. Its rates are those of version 1.1.0, which is the devel a first edition of this report compared against master. It is kept as a reference, because it shows what the cap repairs. (Its statistics equal those of that first run to every stored digit.)

The report asks two questions. Which behaviors got better? And does devel change what eSVD-DE reports on ordinary data, or mostly how it behaves at the edges?

The short answer.

  1. The point estimate did not change. The log2 fold changes of the two versions agree at a Pearson correlation of at least 0.9993 in every regime.
  2. Most of the fixes are corner-case fixes, and they behave as NEWS.md says. Inputs that used to crash deep in the optimizer with missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed, or finish silently with a wrong answer, now stop at the first step with a message that names the problem (section 7).
  3. The nuisance (overdispersion) rate is estimated differently, and with the cap the test is calibrated as master’s was.
    • The estimate. In the regimes where the rate can be estimated, devel puts 96% of genes within twofold of the true rate, against 56% for master.
    • False discoveries. Under the global null, 0.2 of 300 null genes per data set reach FDR < 0.05, against 0.2 under master and 2.7 without the cap.
    • The near-Poisson regime. The type-I error at p < 0.05 is 0.065, against 0.067 for master and 0.28 without the cap.
    • The statistics. The Welch statistics are close to master’s (Pearson r of at least 0.986 in every regime), and putting master’s rates into devel still reproduces master’s statistics, to within 0.006 (section 5.3).
    • What the cap acts on. It acts on 7% to 12% of genes in ordinary data.
  4. The cost is small but visible. On the generate_null() cohorts devel finds 8.1 of 10 DE genes per data set, against 8.8 for master. Elsewhere the two are within simulation noise of each other on false and true discoveries (section 6.2).

1.1 How the comparison was run

The versions are installed into separate private libraries and run in separate R processes. The step-by-step API (initialize_esvd() through compute_pvalue()) has the same function names and arguments in both, except for cap_multiplier, which only 1.2.0 has. So one script drives every version, calling the steps in the order eSVD() runs them. All heavy computation happens in the scripts; this document only reads their CSVs.

Script What it does
00_install_versions_claude.sh git archive 3d5f7bf → lib/master; git archive d49e402 (1.1.0) → lib/devel_1.1.0, used by ../overdispersion_brainstorm/; the working tree (1.2.0) → lib/devel
helpers_claude.R the simulator and the pipeline, shared by the scripts below
01_simulate_data_claude.R 6 regimes × 10 replicates → data/*.rds, and the truth → output/truth.csv
02_run_regimes_claude.R fits all 60 data sets with one version or arm → output/<label>/genes.csv, runs.csv
03_corner_cases_claude.R 12 perturbed cohorts per version → output/<version>/corner_cases.csv
run_all_claude.sh all of the above, end to end

The whole of run_all_claude.sh took 6.4 minutes on the laptop it was run on.

devel_swap is an ablation, not a version. It runs the devel code on each data set, but right after estimate_nuisance() it overwrites the per-gene nuisance rate with the value master estimated on the same data set. Where devel_swap matches master, the nuisance estimate explains the difference between the versions.

1.2 The simulated regimes

Every regime has 20 individuals (10 case, 10 control), 30 cells each, and 300 genes. Except for generate_null, the data come from the eSVD hierarchical model itself, using the generator of .build_tiny_data() in tests/testthat/helper-fixtures.R. That model has:

  • a rank-3 latent structure;
  • an individual-level random effect;
  • Sex and Age effects;
  • a per-cell library size;
  • counts \(A_{ji} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\ell_{ji} \lambda_{ji})\) with \(\lambda_{ji} \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\text{mean} = \mu_{ji}, \text{rate} = \beta_j)\).

The truth for a gene’s log2 fold change is the ratio of the arithmetic means of \(\exp(\text{natural parameter})\) in the two arms. That is what both the logFC and the Welch statistic contrast.

Regime DE genes Nuisance rate \(\beta_j\) What it probes
baseline 15, effect 0.8 (natural log) U(2, 8) on the log scale ordinary data
null 0 U(2, 8) calibration
strong_de 15, effect ±3 U(2, 8) large Welch statistics; the t → z mapping
near_poisson 15, effect 0.8 U(50, 1000) little overdispersion; where the cap binds for almost every gene
minimal_design 15, effect 0.8 U(2, 8) no Sex/Age, so covariates are only Intercept + Log_UMI + CC (the GLM-fallback offset fix)
generate_null 10 the package’s own generate_null() a generator not written for this report

Each regime has 10 replicates with different seeds. The fit uses k = 3, l2pen = 0.1, max_iter = 50, and otherwise the package defaults.

Collinear covariates refused by name 1.0.2 7

3 Point estimates: the log2 fold change

plot_df <- logfc_wide_df
plot_df$regime <- factor(plot_df$regime, levels = regime_levels)
plot1 <- ggplot2::ggplot(plot_df, ggplot2::aes(x = master, y = devel))
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0,
                                      colour = "#c3c2b7", linewidth = 0.5)
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(colour = status),
                                     size = 0.8, alpha = 0.6)
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ regime, nrow = 2, scales = "free")
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = status_col_vec,
                                              name = "True status")
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::labs(x = "master: log2 fold change",
                               y = "devel: log2 fold change",
                               title = "The log2 fold change is essentially unchanged",
                               subtitle = "All 10 replicates per regime; grey line is y = x")
plot(plot1)

agreement_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(regime_levels, function(r){
  x <- logfc_wide_df[logfc_wide_df$regime == r, ]
  data.frame(regime = r,
             pearson = stats::cor(x$master, x$devel),
             median_abs_diff = stats::median(abs(x$master - x$devel)),
             max_abs_diff = max(abs(x$master - x$devel)))
}))
knitr::kable(agreement_df, digits = 4,
             col.names = c("Regime", "Pearson r", "Median |Δ|", "Max |Δ|"),
             caption = "log2 fold change, master vs devel, all genes and replicates.")
log2 fold change, master vs devel, all genes and replicates.
Regime Pearson r Median |Δ| Max |Δ|
baseline 0.9999 0.0018 0.0256
null 0.9993 0.0019 0.0243
strong_de 1.0000 0.0019 0.0683
near_poisson 0.9999 0.0008 0.0437
minimal_design 0.9999 0.0014 0.0250
generate_null 1.0000 0.0001 0.0367

The logFC is log2(case_mean / control_mean), where each mean averages the per-individual posterior means. The posterior mean moves only a little with the nuisance rate, so this estimate is nearly identical across versions. The small differences come from the fit and from the rescaling by bool_stabilize_underdispersion. devel returns this quantity directly as log2fc_vec; for master it is computed from case_mean and control_mean. The two definitions are the same.

minimal_design is where the GLM-fallback offset fix would show, and it does not. With only Intercept + Log_UMI + CC, master fitted the intercepts without the depth offset. That changes the initialization, but after two rounds of opt_esvd() the fold changes agree as closely as in any other regime.

4 The nuisance (overdispersion) estimate

nuisance_vec is the Gamma rate \(\beta_j = 1/\gamma_j\): a large value means little overdispersion, and \(\beta_j \to \infty\) is a Poisson gene.

The three versions compute it as follows:

  • master: gamma_rate searched only up to the gene’s largest library size, so its rate is min(MLE, max_i s_ji).
  • devel_nocap (1.1.0’s rate): the maximum-likelihood estimate itself.
  • devel (1.2.0): max(min(MLE, 10 · m_j), 1e-4 · m_j), with m_j = median_i s_ji. A gene with no finite MLE is set to the cap.

../OVERDISPERSION_BRAINSTORM.md explains why the cap was chosen, and ../overdispersion_brainstorm/overdispersion_cap_claude.html explains it with formulas and plots.

The units trap. The rate shares its units with the fitted library size s_ji, which contains the gene’s intercept. The simulator’s library size averages 1. So the simulator’s rate is not on the fit’s scale. The first edition of this report compared the two directly and concluded that the uncapped estimate was “biased upward two- to threefold”. Most of that was the units. Below, the true rate is multiplied by the gene’s median fitted library size before the comparison.

4.1 Against the truth

plot_df$version <- factor(plot_df$version,
                          levels = c("master", "devel_nocap", "devel"))
plot1 <- ggplot2::ggplot(plot_df, ggplot2::aes(x = nuisance_true_fit,
                                               y = nuisance))

}))

What the plot and tables show:

  • master’s estimates are nearly independent of the truth (Spearman near 0). Its rate is min(MLE, max_i s_ji), and in these regimes nearly every gene sits at that bound (78% to 100%, ../OVERDISPERSION_BRAINSTORM.md section 2.1). What master reports is close to the largest library size of the gene, not a property of its overdispersion. In near_poisson, where the true rates are far above any library size, it is two orders of magnitude too small.
  • The MLE (devel_nocap) is accurate where a finite estimate exists: its median ratio to the truth is 1.04 to 1.16 in the four ordinary regimes. But a few genes per data set have no finite MLE and run to about 1e7, and in near_poisson about half of them do.
  • The cap keeps the MLE’s accuracy and removes the divergence. In the ordinary regimes it acts on about a tenth of the genes, and it raises the share within twofold of the truth from about 89% to about 95%. In near_poisson no version recovers the rate: those genes are close to Poisson, the likelihood is flat, and every estimate is a bound.

4.2 Why the nuisance matters downstream

The posterior shrinks each cell’s observed count toward the fitted mean, with a weight governed by \(\beta_j\). A huge \(\beta_j\) makes the posterior collapse onto the fitted mean. The within-individual posterior variance then vanishes, the denominator of the Welch statistic shrinks, and the statistic grows. The cap bounds how far that collapse can go.

With the cap, devel’s statistics are closer to master’s than the uncapped ones were. The correlation with master rises from the fourth column (devel_nocap) to the second (devel) in every regime, and the typical gene moves by a few hundredths.

5.3 The ablation: the nuisance estimate is the whole difference

Put master’s nuisance rates into the devel code and the Welch statistics match master’s in every regime, to within 0.006, and to all six stored digits in most regimes. The other changes between the versions move nothing that reaches the statistic in these regimes:

  • the reparameterization by QR;
  • the offset in the GLM fallback;
  • the deterministic SVD start;
  • the rewritten empirical-null estimators.

What remains between master and devel is therefore the difference between two bounds on the rate: master’s max_i s_ji, which most genes sit at, and devel’s 10 · median_i s_ji, which about a tenth of them sit at.

plot_df <- teststat_wide_df[teststat_wide_df$regime %in%
                              c("baseline", "null", "near_poisson"), ]
plot_df$regime <- factor(plot_df$regime, levels = regime_levels)
plot1 <- ggplot2::ggplot(plot_df, ggplot2::aes(x = master, y = devel_swap))
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0,
                                      colour = "#c3c2b7", linewidth = 0.5)
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::geom_point(colour = version_col_vec[["devel_swap"]],
                                     size = 0.8, alpha = 0.6)
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ regime, nrow = 1, scales = "free")
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::labs(x = "master: Welch statistic",
                               y = "devel with master's nuisance: Welch statistic",
                               title = "devel_swap reproduces master")
plot(plot1)

6 Calibration and power

6.1 Null genes: p-value QQ plots

The p-values below are the ones each version reports, measured against its estimated empirical null. Each panel pools the null genes of all 10 replicates.

qq_list <- list()
for(r in regime_levels){
  for(v in c("master", "devel_nocap", "devel")){
    p_vec <- gene_df$p[gene_df$regime == r & gene_df$version == v &
                         !gene_df$is_de]
    p_vec <- sort(p_vec)
    qq_list[[paste(r, v)]] <- data.frame(regime = r,
                                         version = v,
                                         expected = -log10(stats::ppoints(length(p_vec))),
                                         observed = -log10(p_vec))
  }
}
qq_df <- do.call(rbind, qq_list)
qq_df$regime <- factor(qq_df$regime, levels = regime_levels)
qq_df$version <- factor(qq_df$version,
                        levels = c("master", "devel_nocap", "devel"))
plot1 <- ggplot2::ggplot(qq_df, ggplot2::aes(x = expected, y = observed))
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0,
                                      colour = "#52514e", linewidth = 0.5,
                                      linetype = "dashed")
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(colour = version),
                                     size = 0.8, alpha = 0.7)
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ regime, nrow = 2, scales = "free_y")
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = version_col_vec,
                                              name = "Version")
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::labs(x = "Expected −log10 p (uniform)",
                               y = "Observed −log10 p, null genes",
                               title = "The cap brings devel's null tail back to master's; without it the tail is heavy")
plot(plot1)

6.2 False and true discoveries at FDR < 0.05

discovery_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(regime_levels, function(r){
  do.call(rbind, lapply(version_vec, function(v){
    x <- gene_df[gene_df$regime == r & gene_df$version == v, ]
    sig_vec <- x$fdr < 0.05
    data.frame(regime = r,
               version = v,
               type1 = mean(x$p[!x$is_de] < 0.05),
               fp = sum(sig_vec & !x$is_de) / 10,

               num_de = sum(x$is_de) / 10,
               fdp = sum(sig_vec & !x$is_de) / max(1, sum(sig_vec)))
  }))
}))

fp_list <- list()
for(r in regime_levels){
  for(v in c("master", "devel_nocap", "devel")){
    for(i in 1:10){
      idx <- gene_df$regime == r & gene_df$version == v & gene_df$rep == i
      fp_list[[paste(r, v, i)]] <- data.frame(regime = r,
                                              version = v,
                                              rep = i,
                                              fp = sum(gene_df$fdr[idx] < 0.05 &
                                                         !gene_df$is_de[idx]))
    }
  }
}
fp_df <- do.call(rbind, fp_list)
fp_df$regime <- factor(fp_df$regime, levels = regime_levels)
fp_df$version <- factor(fp_df$version,
                        levels = c("master", "devel_nocap", "devel"))
plot1 <- ggplot2::ggplot(fp_df, ggplot2::aes(x = version, y = fp + 1))
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(colour = version),
                                     position = ggplot2::position_jitter(width = 0.15,
                                                                         height = 0,
                                                                         seed = 1),
                                     size = 2)
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ regime, nrow = 1)
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::scale_y_log10()
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = version_col_vec,
                                              guide = "none")
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::theme(axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(angle = 45,
                                                                    hjust = 1))
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::labs(x = NULL,
                               y = "False discoveries + 1 (log scale)",
                               title = "False discoveries per data set at FDR < 0.05",
                               subtitle = "One point per replicate")
plot(plot1)

What this shows:

  • At p < 0.05 the null genes are calibrated in devel and master in every regime (type-I error 0.03 to 0.07). Without the cap, near_poisson was at 0.28.
  • In the far tail, where FDR control acts, devel and master are within simulation noise of each other.
    • devel has slightly more false discoveries in baseline, minimal_design and strong_de (0.3 to 0.4 more per data set).
    • It has slightly fewer in near_poisson and generate_null.
    • The standard error of these per-data-set counts is about 0.5, so none of the differences is resolved.
    • Without the cap, false discoveries were 2 to 19 times master’s in five regimes, and 63 per data set (24 times master’s) in near_poisson.
  • Power is the same except on generate_null(), where devel finds 8.1 of 10 DE genes against master’s 8.8. Without the cap it found 8.2. So the loss comes from estimating the rate rather than capping it at master’s bound, not from the cap itself.
  • master is not “right” in the sense of estimating anything. Its rates ignore the truth (section 4.1). Treating every gene as moderately overdispersed happens to be conservative, and the cap reaches the same calibration while letting nine genes in ten keep their own estimate.

6.3 Where devel’s false discoveries come from

The table splits the null genes of devel by their nuisance_status, and the null genes of devel_nocap by whether their rate diverged.

nocap_df <- gene_df[gene_df$version == "devel_nocap", ]
status_fp_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(regime_levels, function(r){
  x <- devel_df[devel_df$regime == r & !devel_df$is_de, ]
  y <- nocap_df[nocap_df$regime == r & !nocap_df$is_de, ]
  .rate <- function(z, idx){
    if(!any(idx)) return(NA)
    mean(z$fdr[idx] < 0.05)
  }
  data.frame(regime = r,
             fp_estimated = .rate(x, x$nuisance_status == "estimated"),
             fp_capped = .rate(x, x$nuisance_status == "capped"),
             fp_boundary = .rate(x, x$nuisance_status == "boundary"),
             fp_nocap_diverged = .rate(y, y$nuisance > 1e4),
             fp_nocap_other = .rate(y, y$nuisance <= 1e4))
}))

                               y = "|Welch statistic|",

                               subtitle = "All null genes of 10 replicates")
plot(plot1)

  • Without the cap, a diverged rate was close to a guaranteed false discovery in the ordinary regimes. Each such gene was almost always an error.
  • With the cap, no boundary gene is a false discovery in the ordinary regimes. The false discoveries that remain are spread over estimated and capped genes, at under 2% of null genes of either status. Capped genes carry a somewhat higher share than estimated ones: they are the genes nearest the bound, and the bound still gives them less posterior variance than most.

6.4 The t → z mapping (NEWS: “no longer produces an infinite statistic”)

master computed the Gaussian statistic as qnorm(pt(T, df)), which returns Inf once pt() rounds to 1. devel works on the log scale. Applying the old mapping to each arm’s statistics shows where it would have failed:

tz_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("master", "devel_nocap", "devel"), function(v){
  x <- gene_df[gene_df$version == v, ]
  z_old_vec <- stats::qnorm(stats::pt(x$teststat, df = x$df))
  data.frame(version = v,
             max_teststat = max(x$teststat),
             num_inf_old_mapping = sum(!is.finite(z_old_vec)),
             num_nonfinite_reported = sum(!is.finite(x$gaussian_teststat)))
}))
knitr::kable(tz_df, digits = 1,
             col.names = c("Statistics from", "Largest Welch statistic",
                           "Inf under master's mapping",
                           "Non-finite z actually reported"),
             caption = "All 60 data sets.")
All 60 data sets.
Statistics from Largest Welch statistic Inf under master’s mapping Non-finite z actually reported
master 26.1 0 0
devel_nocap 52.9 10 0
devel 26.2 0 0

With the cap, devel’s largest statistic is back near master’s (about 26, in strong_de), and the old mapping would not have overflowed on these data. The log-scale mapping remains the correct computation; the uncapped rate was what made it necessary in practice.

6.5 Which empirical-null estimator ran

devel records this; master does not (method is NA).

                          levels = c("master", "devel_nocap", "devel"))

plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(colour = version),
                                     position = ggplot2::position_jitter(width = 0.15,
                                                                         height = 0,
                                                                         seed = 1),
                                     size = 2)
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ regime, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y")
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = version_col_vec,
                                              guide = "none")

                                                                    hjust = 1))

                               title = "Empirical-null SD per replicate")
plot(plot1)

locfdr converges more often under the cap than without it. The fallback to the truncated MLE is now mostly in strong_de, where the DE genes’ large statistics distort the spline fit. devel warns when it falls back; master may have fallen back as often, but had no way to report it. In near_poisson the uncapped arm’s null SD was more than twice master’s, and the cap brings it back.

7 Corner cases

Each row below perturbs one small cohort (10 individuals × 30 cells, 100 genes, 10 DE) and runs the full pipeline. “silent” means the pipeline finished without warnings.

case_vec <- unique(corner_df$case)
corner_wide_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(case_vec, function(cs){
  m <- corner_df[corner_df$case == cs & corner_df$version == "master", ]
  d <- corner_df[corner_df$case == cs & corner_df$version == "devel", ]
  .describe <- function(x){
    txt <- x$outcome
    if(x$outcome == "error") txt <- paste0("**error** in ", x$error)
    if(x$outcome == "warning") txt <- paste0("warning: ", x$warnings)
    if(!is.na(x$num_sig)) txt <- paste0(txt, " — ", x$num_sig, " genes at FDR < 0.05")
    if(!is.na(x$metric_value)) txt <- paste0(txt, "; ", x$metric_name, " = ",
                                             signif(x$metric_value, 3))
    substr(txt, 1, 330)
  }
  data.frame(Case = paste0("`", cs, "`: ", d$description),
             master = .describe(m),
             devel = .describe(d))
}))

             caption = "Behavior of each version on the perturbed cohorts. Messages truncated.")

sparse_na: One NA among the nonzero entries of a dgCMatrix error in initialize_esvd: missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed error in initialize_esvd: covariates contains NA or non-finite entries
all_zero_gene: Two genes are all-zero warning: from glmnet C++ code (error code -1); Convergence for 1th lambda value not reached after maxit=100000 iterations; solutions for larger lambdas returned || an empty model has been returned; probably a convergence issue — 9 genes at FDR < 0.05 error in initialize_esvd: 2 gene(s) are all zero (gene3, gene50); remove them before initialization, or run eSVD_helper, which removes them and records the removal in gene_status
collinear_covariate: A covariate column duplicated (Age twice) error in opt_esvd (first): missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed error in initialize_esvd: covariates is rank deficient (rank 5 for 6 columns): Age_copy can be written as a combination of the other columns. Remove one variable from each collinear set. Including an indicator for every individual, or for every level of a factor, causes this
confounded_design: Sex identical to case-control status error in opt_esvd (first): missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed error in initialize_esvd: covariates is rank deficient (rank 4 for 5 columns): Sex_M can be written as a combination of the other columns. Remove one variable from each collinear set. Including an indicator for every individual, or for every level of a factor, causes this
few_genes: Only 30 genes silent — 30 genes at FDR < 0.05 warning: locfdr could not estimate the empirical null; using the truncated_mle estimator instead (null_mean = -0.1409, null_sd = 1.174). This usually means too few genes for locfdr’s spline fit — 0 genes at FDR < 0.05
extreme_de: 5 genes up-regulated by exp(4), nearly Poisson silent — 5 genes at FDR < 0.05; largest Gaussian statistic = 5.04 warning: locfdr could not estimate the empirical null; using the truncated_mle estimator instead (null_mean = -1.993, null_sd = 0.4051). This usually means too few genes for locfdr’s spline fit — 5 genes at FDR < 0.05; largest Gaussian statistic = 5.04
one_case_individual: The case arm has a single individual error in compute_pvalue: missing values and NaN’s not allowed if ‘na.rm’ is FALSE error in compute_test_statistic: each arm needs at least 2 individuals to form a two-sample test; found 1 case and 5 control. With one individual in an arm the Welch degrees of freedom are 0 and every p-value is NaN
two_cell_individual: One control individual has only 2 cells silent — 10 genes at FDR < 0.05 error in compute_test_statistic: individual(s) indiv1 (2 cells) have fewer than 3 cells. Remove them upstream (see eSVD_helper), or pass min_cells_per_individual = 0 to proceed anyway
individual_in_both_arms: Half of one individual’s cells labelled case, half control error in compute_test_statistic: length(intersect(control_individuals, case_individuals)) == 0 is not TRUE error in compute_test_statistic: length(intersect(control_individuals, case_individuals)) == 0 is not TRUE

Reading the table:

  • Fixed, and clearly better.
    • collinear_covariate and confounded_design (Sex identical to case-control status) used to fail two stages later with missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed from opt_esvd(). Now they stop in initialize_esvd(), which names the redundant column.
    • all_zero_gene used to finish with glmnet convergence warnings and fit the zero genes anyway. Now it is refused by name and pointed at eSVD_helper().
    • one_case_individual used to die in compute_pvalue() on NaNs. Now it stops in compute_test_statistic() with an explanation.
    • two_cell_individual used to run silently. Now it is refused, and can be overridden with min_cells_per_individual = 0.
  • few_genes is the most striking row. With 30 genes, master declared every gene significant, silently: its unconstrained fallback estimator gave a degenerate empirical null. devel calls nothing significant. Under 1.1.0, locfdr converged on this cohort; under the cap it does not, and devel falls back to the truncated MLE and says so in a warning. The answer is the same either way.
  • The reference cohort finds 10 genes at FDR < 0.05 under devel, as under master. Under 1.1.0 it found 13, which included false discoveries.
  • Unchanged. individual_in_both_arms is refused by the same stopifnot() in both versions. The friendlier check lives in eSVD(), which these scripts do not call.
  • determinism: devel is bit-identical across two fits after different set.seed() calls. sparse_input agrees with dense input in both versions.
  • sparse_na shows a gap between NEWS.md and behavior.
    • NEWS says initialize_esvd() now zeroes NA counts in sparse matrices, but the pipeline never gets that far.
    • format_covariates() computes Log_UMI = log(rowSums(dat)), which is NA for that cell, and initialize_esvd() then stops on the covariates.
    • The error is clearer than master’s (covariates contains NA, against missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed). But it names the covariates rather than the count that caused them.
    • The zeroing only helps a caller who builds the covariates some other way.
  • extreme_de (five genes up by \(e^4\) on nearly Poisson genes): both versions find the five genes, and neither overflowed at this size. devel warns because locfdr falls back.

8 New since 1.1.0: a standard error for the log2 fold change

master has no counterpart. Below, the interval logFC ± 2 SE is checked against the true log2 fold change. For devel it is split by nuisance_status, and for devel_nocap by whether the rate diverged.

.cover <- function(x, idx){
  if(!any(idx)) return(NA)
  mean(abs(x$logFC[idx] - x$truth_log2fc[idx]) <= 2 * x$logFC_se[idx])
}
se_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(regime_levels, function(r){
  x <- devel_df[devel_df$regime == r, ]
  y <- nocap_df[nocap_df$regime == r, ]
  data.frame(regime = r,
             cover_estimated = .cover(x, x$nuisance_status == "estimated"),
             cover_capped = .cover(x, x$nuisance_status == "capped"),
             cover_boundary = .cover(x, x$nuisance_status == "boundary"),
             cover_nocap_diverged = .cover(y, y$nuisance > 1e4),
             median_se = stats::median(x$logFC_se))
}))
knitr::kable(se_df, digits = 3,
             col.names = c("Regime", "devel: estimated", "devel: capped",
                           "devel: boundary", "devel_nocap: rate > 1e4",
                           "devel: median SE"),
             caption = "Coverage of ±2 SE, all genes and replicates.")

null 0.999 0.997 1.000 0.474 0.370

                                  levels = names(nuisance_status_col_vec))

plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0,
                                      colour = "#c3c2b7", linewidth = 0.5)
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::geom_errorbar(ggplot2::aes(ymin = logFC - 2 * logFC_se,
                                                     ymax = logFC + 2 * logFC_se,
                                                     colour = nuisance_status),
                                        width = 0, alpha = 0.5)

                                     size = 1.2)

                                              name = NULL, drop = FALSE)
plot1 <- plot1 + ggplot2::labs(x = "True log2 fold change",
                               y = "devel: log2 fold change ± 2 SE",
                               title = "baseline, replicate 1")
plot(plot1)

Under the cap the SE covers the truth at or above the nominal rate for genes of every status, in five of the six regimes. It is conservative, because the within-individual term dominates. Without the cap, genes whose rate diverged had coverage well below nominal: their interval collapsed with the posterior variance. This answers, in simulation, the part of Q-LFC-1 that asked whether the cap repairs the SE.

The exception is strong_de (coverage about 0.85 for estimated genes, and lower for capped ones), with or without the cap. There, the ±3 effects move each case cell’s total count, so the Log_UMI depth adjustment shifts every gene’s fold change. That is a bias, which an SE cannot absorb.

9 Runtime

runtime_df <- stats::aggregate(seconds ~ regime + version, data = run_df,
                               FUN = stats::median)
runtime_wide_df <- stats::reshape(runtime_df, idvar = "regime",
                                  timevar = "version", direction = "wide")
colnames(runtime_wide_df) <- sub("^seconds\\.", "", colnames(runtime_wide_df))
knitr::kable(runtime_wide_df, digits = 2,

devel is about a third slower than master on these small fits (about 0.6 s per fit). The cap itself costs nothing measurable (devel against devel_nocap). The rest has not been profiled.

10 Verdict

  • On the estimate researchers report first, the fold change, nothing changed.
  • On the test, devel 1.2.0 is calibrated as master was, and its nuisance rate means something.
    • master was calibrated by accident, through a bound at the largest library size that held nearly every gene.
    • 1.1.0 removed that bound and paid for it with false discoveries: 2.7 per 300 null genes under the null, and 63 in near_poisson.
    • 1.2.0 bounds the rate deliberately at 10 times the median library size. False discoveries return to master’s level, within noise, while about nine genes in ten keep their own estimate and the estimates track the truth (Spearman about 0.6 against about 0).
    • The ablation still attributes every difference in the statistics to the nuisance rate.
  • The cost is a small loss of power on the generate_null() cohorts (0.7 of 10 DE genes per data set), and, at most, a few tenths of a false discovery per data set in the ordinary regimes, which the ten replicates cannot resolve.
  • Everything else in NEWS.md behaves as a corner-case fix, and in those corners devel is clearly better: clear, early errors instead of deep crashes, and no silent “everything is significant” on small gene sets.

11 What we glossed over

  • Only simulated data, and mostly data from the eSVD model itself.
    • The one outside generator (generate_null()) is also where devel loses a little power.
    • The default cap_multiplier = 10 was chosen on simulations like these (../OVERDISPERSION_BRAINSTORM.md, section 3.3), so they are not a held-out test of it.
    • One real data set is the open check (Idea 11 of the brainstorm).
  • 300 genes, 20 individuals, 30 cells per individual. Chosen to fit the 30-minute budget. The false-discovery counts scale with the number of genes; the rates are what to compare. With ten replicates the SE of a per-data-set count is about 0.5.
  • The median library size is between 0.8 and 2.5 in every regime, because the fit’s library includes the gene intercept. With bool_library_includes_interept = FALSE it would be in the thousands. That is where 1.2.0’s rule that a boundary gene goes to the cap itself (and not to the optimizer’s stopping value) matters, and it was not exercised here.
  • eSVD() itself was not run, because it needs a Seurat object. The scripts call its steps in the same order and with its defaults, except k = 3 and max_iter = 50. So compute_test_per_gene() (the bool_diet = TRUE path), recompute_pvalue() and the diagnostic plots were not compared here; the package’s tests cover them.
  • master is not bit-reproducible across runs on generate_null(). Between the first edition of this report and this one, master’s Welch statistics on those cohorts moved by up to 0.006 on identical data, while devel’s did not move. This is the random SVD start that devel fixed, and it is why the ablation agrees to 0.006 rather than to every digit there.
  • The rescaling by bool_stabilize_underdispersion divides every rate by their geometric mean when that mean is above 1. It is on in every arm. Diverged genes inflated that mean under 1.1.0, and the cap bounds it. Its separate contribution was not isolated.
